newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia Gold - Sentiment mixed as options expiry looms.
newsitem.headline: Asia Gold - Sentiment mixed as options expiry looms.

text.p: Asian bullion dealers had mixed views on gold's near-term direction, as the metal ended the week on a quiet note, eyeing the New York Comex options expiry later on Friday.
Hong Kong spot gold was trading at US$353.00/40 an ounce at about 1200 (0400 GMT), a shade down from its opening of $353.30/80.
Some dealers said market sentiment was bearish after the Swiss government's plan to sell some gold reserves over a 10 year period to fund a Holocaust's victims fund.
But others in the British colony were more optimistic, partly due to the upcoming options expiry.
"There may be some action after the options expiry," said one bullion dealer.
"It's probably looking a little more positive than anything, there's a chance it may break higher next week," said the precious metals head at an international bank.
"The medium term is quite bullish," another dealer said, noting that U.S. funds wanted to keep short positions and cover if the dollar dipped.
Spot gold's short term was seen at between $351-$354 an ounce, at least until the options expiry, dealers in Singapore and Hong Kong said.
"It'll be a range market. There's fairly strong support at $350.50 (an ounce)," a bank trader in Singapore said.
But some dealers said even if gold skipped up next week, there was good selling interest at $356 per ounce.

As gold climbed through February and the beginning of March from $336 to $360 per ounce, operators covered their shorts and turned long, but were discouraged when the market refused to hold in the $360s, another senior Hong Kong bullion trader said.
"It's always justified to be short," he said.

Physical gold demand in Asia has slowed with the end of the Chinese Lunar New Year and Hari Raya peak season, but premiums are likely stay firm in a range-bound market, precious metal dealers in Singapore said.

"Despite the weaker price, demand is just not as strong as it was a month ago," a senior dealer for a Singapore-based bank said. "The buying is coming from the same general region like the Chinese areas, but I think a lot of it is for re-export."
"The regional buyers are waiting for the prices to come off some more," another Singapore dealer said.
One jeweller expected the demand to continue slowing with most fund managers preferring to put money in stocks and bonds than in precious metals.
Singapore premiums firmed marginally to between 140-150 U.S. cents over spot London prices from last week's 120-140 cents as supplies of kilobars in the city-state remained tight.
Recent physical demand in Hong Kong was said to be slow, as the market had hovered above $350 an ounce and below $355 for a while now, and end-users were unwilling to buy at these levels.
Hong Kong premiums, which touched 170 U.S. cents last month, had softened to around 120-130 U.S. cents and are likely to drop to around the 100 U.S. cents level in the near term.

"When the price goes up, producers try to sell more than before, so the premiums will drop slightly," one dealer said. -- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358 -- Rene Pastor, Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
